units.text: App Mesh support ended on September thirtieth, twenty twenty-six. The design questions remain: how do services route traffic, establish identity, observe calls and handle failures? Consider ECS Service Connect for participating ECS services, VPC Lattice for connectivity across VPCs and accounts, or a supported Kubernetes mesh when its features fit. Verify traffic policy, telemetry and TLS rather than assuming these choices are interchangeable.

Follow the caller from its VPC through a Lattice service network to the target in another VPC. Association provides a service access path; routing uses registered targets. When A W S I A M authorization is configured, access also depends on the applicable auth policy and a signed request. Check target health and access logs independently of association.

Trace this caller through three checks: a reachable service network, authorization when A W S I A M mode is enabled, and a listener routing to a healthy target. A denied request calls for a review of identity, policy and signing. A target failure calls for a look at health and routing. Use Lattice access logs and metrics to tell these cases apart.

Start with what tenants are allowed to share. A silo dedicates resources for stronger isolation; a pool shares them, demanding tenant-scoped controls. A bridge shares selected layers but dedicates others where the requirement justifies it. Derive tenant context from trusted authentication and document the blast radius and recovery ownership at each layer.

Pick the boundary by trust and failure impact. Separate accounts or clusters can reduce shared blast radius. A pooled application must authorize the tenant before touching its data. A bridge may keep shared ingress but use dedicated data stores. A tenant identifier supplied by the caller is not proof of authorization; enforce the boundary with trusted context.

A namespace groups Kubernetes resources, but the workloads can still share nodes and a kernel. Add scoped roles and service accounts, enforced network policy, quotas, admission controls and workload I A M. Where trust or blast radius demands more separation, consider dedicated nodes, clusters or accounts. Test both data isolation and resource contention instead of assuming a namespace name ensures either.

In this sandbox rollout, establish two healthy old tasks and verify the load balancer and a real response. Deploy the new revision with a strategy that keeps healthy capacity while replacements become ready. Confirm new target and application health before retiring the old tasks. A deliberate sandbox health failure lets you observe deployment events and practice recovery or rollback.

Use an authorized test repository. Record the trusted image digest and check findings, access and tag settings. Preview lifecycle rules before cleanup; the known-good rollback digest must still be pullable. If replication is in scope, verify the destination digest separately, and capture evidence before removing sandbox resources.

When a sandbox Pod is Pending, start with its events. In this example the scheduler reports insufficient CPU. Adjust an unrealistic request only if it is safe, or add eligible node capacity; then confirm readiness and a successful request. Image pull errors and failed health checks need other fixes, so follow what the observed event actually says.

Prove both sides of the sandbox isolation boundary. With a test identity for Tenant A, verify its own expected access works and a request for Tenant B's test data is denied. Check app authorization, workload I A M and enforced network policy separately. Record the expected decision and supporting evidence, then clean up test data and resources.

An uploaded image triggers Lambda through an S three event. The function makes a thumbnail and writes it to a separate bucket, so the output does not depend on the execution environment surviving. On-demand Lambda Event Functions can run up to thirty minutes per invocation. A W S operates the compute; the application owns the code, scoped permissions and safe handling of repeat events.

An EventBridge event invokes the handler in a Lambda execution environment. Initialization can be reused, but a later invocation may get a replacement environment. Keep durable results in a service such as DynamoDB or S three, not process memory. Verify input, give the function only needed permissions and design both repeat processing and downstream capacity deliberately.

Suppose EventBridge delivers the same product update again after a retry. A warm environment might remember handling it, but a replacement would not. Make the write idempotent against durable state so the outcome stays correct in either case. Reusing an initialized client helps performance, not correctness.

A ZIP package can use a supported managed runtime. A Lambda image is a compatible Linux image for one architecture, stored in ECR, that implements the Lambda Runtime API. The runtime interface client is how compatible images do that. An arbitrary web-server image is not automatically suitable; a long-running server may fit ECS instead. Patch dependencies regardless of packaging.
